knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ (2x+y)+(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y}\right)}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 0+1}{0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{0+1}{0-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x+7}+\sqrt{y+2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+7)^{1/2}+(y+2)^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{1}{2}(x+7)^{-1/2}+\frac{1}{2}(y+2)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(y+2)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2}(x+7)^{-1/2} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y+2}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+7}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{y+2}}{\sqrt{x+7}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\,7)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,7)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{\sqrt{y+2}}{\sqrt{x+7}}\right)|}_{(2,\,7)} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{7+2}}{\sqrt{2+7}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{3}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}y & =4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x) \\ 3{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 \\ {x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4-3{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4-3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{4-3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}}\right)|}_{(1,4)} \\  & =\frac{4-3(1)^{2}(4)}{(1)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(-8)}{1} \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\,2)$ for the curve $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =0 \\ y(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\,2)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(\pi /3,\,2)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\right)}_{(\pi /3,\,2)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,\,4)$ for the curve $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}+{y}^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(4,\,4)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =-{\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{4}}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,1)$ for the curve $5{x}^{3}-2{y}^{4}=3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{3}-2{y}^{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{4}) & =0 \\ 15{x}^{2}-8{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -8{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-15{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{15{x}^{2}}{8{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{15{x}^{2}}{8{y}^{3}}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{15\cdot {1}^{2}}{8\cdot {1}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y & =6x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ [3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}]-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ (3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,0)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}\right)}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & =\frac{6-2\cdot 0\cdot {0}^{3}}{3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{6}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}-{y}^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(9,\,4)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(9,\,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}\right)|}_{(9,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+[2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}]-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ (6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y}\right)|}_{(1,1)} \\  & =\frac{3(1)^{2}-2(1)(1)^{2}}{6(1)^{2}+2(1)^{2}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}y=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ for the curve $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)=\sqrt{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{2}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,2)$ for the curve $3x^2+2y^3=19.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, differentiate the curve implicitly with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$. The chain rule supplies a factor of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ when differentiating $y^3$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(3x^2+2y^3)&=\frac{d}{dx}(19)\\
6x+6y^2\frac{dy}{dx}&=0\\
6y^2\frac{dy}{dx}&=-6x\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{x}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now evaluate the derivative at $(1,2)$:

$$
m=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,2)}=-\frac{1}{2^2}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$. Use the product rule on $xy$ and the chain rule on $y^2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(xy+y^2)&=\frac{d}{dx}(x^2-1)\\
x\frac{dy}{dx}+y+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=2x\\
(x+2y)\frac{dy}{dx}&=2x-y\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{2x-y}{x+2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(2,1)$, the denominator is $2+2(1)=4$, so the slope is finite. Substituting gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(2,1)}\\
&=\frac{2(2)-1}{2+2(1)}\\
&=\frac{3}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$. The term $xe^{xy}$ needs the product rule. Inside the exponential, $xy$ also needs the product rule:

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad
\frac{d}{dx}(e^{xy})=e^{xy}\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right).
$$

Differentiate the curve and collect all terms containing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(xe^{xy}+y^2)&=\frac{d}{dx}(e+1)\\
e^{xy}+xe^{xy}\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right)+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=0\\
e^{xy}+xye^{xy}+x^2e^{xy}\frac{dy}{dx}+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=0\\
(x^2e^{xy}+2y)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-e^{xy}(1+xy)\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{e^{xy}(1+xy)}{x^2e^{xy}+2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(1,1)$, $e^{xy}=e$ and the denominator $e+2$ is positive. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,1)}\\
&=-\frac{e(1+1)}{e+2}\\
&=-\frac{2e}{e+2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
